# Conti Ransomware: RaaS Structure, Leak-Derived Insights, and Public Law-Enforcement Attribution

## Executive summary

Public reporting describes Conti as a highly organized ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation that combined malware development, intrusion activity, affiliate relationships, extortion, and administrative functions. The available sources portray Conti not simply as a malware strain, but as a commercially structured criminal enterprise whose operators developed and maintained ransomware while affiliates or other external actors helped conduct intrusions and obtain initial access.

The February–March 2022 disclosure of Conti’s internal chats provided unusually detailed evidence of that organization. The leaked communications reportedly included hundreds of JSON files, internal discussions, screenshots, operational information, development conversations, recruitment exchanges, salary negotiations, and references to distinct personnel functions. Rapid7 characterized the leaks as evidence that Conti operated in ways resembling a software company, while the Center for Internet Security (CIS) emphasized the commercialization of cybercrime and the division of labor among coders, testers, administrators, reverse engineers, penetration testers, and externally contracted spamming personnel ([Rapid7, 2022/2024](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); [Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization)).

The public attribution record is layered. The U.S. Department of State’s Rewards for Justice (RFJ) program assesses that Conti, also known as Wizard Spider, was a Russian government-linked RaaS group and identifies five online aliases—“Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis”—as malicious cyber actors believed to be linked to Conti. Separately, a U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) page identifies Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov, and Oleksii Lytvynenko as defendants in Conti-related criminal cases. The supplied evidence does not establish that any of those defendants used one of the five RFJ aliases. That distinction is important: the RFJ page supplies an alias-to-Conti attribution assessment, while the DOJ page supplies defendant-to-charged-Conti-activity information ([Rewards for Justice, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); [U.S. Attorney’s Office, Middle District of Tennessee, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2)).

## Sources and evidentiary hierarchy

The source set contains four distinct public records, with repeated copies of the same three substantive pages. The repeated entries have been consolidated rather than treated as independent corroboration.

| Source ID | Source | Evidentiary role |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | Rewards for Justice, “Conti” | Government attribution assessment, aliases, victim-impact description, reward notice |
| S2 | Rapid7, “Conti Ransomware Group Internal Chats Leaked Over Russia-Ukraine Conflict” | Technical and threat-intelligence analysis of leaked chats |
| S3 | Center for Internet Security, “The Conti Leaks: A Case of Cybercrime’s Commercialization” | Analysis of organizational structure, commercialization, and MS-ISAC reporting |
| S4 | DOJ, Middle District of Tennessee, “Conti Ransomware” | Official case page identifying defendants, charges, victim information, and procedural updates |

The strongest evidence for formal attribution and legal status comes from S1 and S4 because they are U.S. government sources. S2 and S3 are valuable analytical sources, particularly for interpreting the leaked communications, but they describe assessments and reporting rather than judicial findings. The distinction between a government assessment, a threat-intelligence conclusion, and a criminal charge must therefore be preserved.

## Conti as a ransomware-as-a-service operation

### The RaaS model

The sources describe Conti as a RaaS organization that used a division between malware developers and actors responsible for intrusions. CIS explains that RaaS groups lease or provide malware capabilities to affiliates, who conduct intrusions and share proceeds with the developers. In the model described by CIS, affiliates can obtain or exploit access to victim environments while the core operators concentrate on malware development, infrastructure, coordination, and revenue generation ([Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization)).

This structure is significant because it converts ransomware from an individual attack technique into a scalable service model. The developers do not necessarily need to perform every intrusion themselves. Instead, access brokers, affiliates, and specialized personnel can perform different stages of the operation. CIS specifically describes initial-access brokers as actors who sell established access to victim environments, thereby allowing ransomware affiliates to begin operations without independently completing the initial compromise ([Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization)).

The available material supports the conclusion that Conti’s RaaS model relied on specialization and revenue-sharing rather than a single undifferentiated group of attackers. However, the sources do not provide a complete contractual record for every affiliate, nor do they establish that every attack attributed to Conti followed exactly the same workflow.

### Double extortion and victim pressure

RFJ describes Conti’s operational pattern as involving both data theft and encryption. Operators reportedly stole victims’ files and encrypted servers and workstations, then demanded payment. If a victim refused, the stolen information could be sold or published on a site controlled by the actors. This is the characteristic double-extortion model: denial of access through encryption is combined with the threat of public disclosure ([Rewards for Justice, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/)).

RFJ states that ransom demands varied significantly and could reach as high as $25 million. It also reports that Conti ransomware was used in more than 1,000 operations targeting U.S. and international critical infrastructure and that more than 400 organizations worldwide were victimized, including more than 290 in the United States. The DOJ provides a separate figure, stating that Conti affected more than 900 businesses, nonprofits, governments, and other victims in the United States and elsewhere ([Rewards for Justice, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); [U.S. Attorney’s Office, Middle District of Tennessee, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2)).

These figures should not be mechanically added together. They likely represent different counting methods—operations, organizations, or victims—and may have been published at different times. The appropriate conclusion is that all sources characterize Conti as a large-scale operation with hundreds of victims and a substantial critical-infrastructure impact.

## What the leaks exposed about Conti’s internal structure

### The 2022 disclosure

Rapid7 reports that, on February 27, 2022, the account known as “ContiLeaks” released a large collection of Conti chat logs following Conti’s public support for the Russian government after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The initial archive reportedly contained approximately 14 megabytes of material distributed across 393 JSON files. Rapid7 cautioned that some messages were encrypted and therefore the record was incomplete ([Rapid7, 2022/2024](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/)).

The leak’s context matters. According to Rapid7, internal disagreement followed Conti’s political statement: some members supported Ukraine, and Conti later revised its public position. Rapid7 observed that the organization temporarily took down exposed infrastructure after the disclosure but reported a resumption of normal operations by March 9, 2022. These observations support the conclusion that the leak disrupted operations but did not immediately eliminate the group’s capabilities ([Rapid7, 2022/2024](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/)).

### Specialized personnel and business functions

The leaked communications reportedly showed distinct personnel categories and business functions. CIS identifies “Coders” who wrote malicious code and integrated technologies; “Testers” who evaluated payload performance against security products; “Administrators”; “Reverse Engineers”; and “Penetration Testers/Hackers.” Spamming functions were reportedly contracted outside the core organization. CIS further reports an insider estimate that Conti employed more than 60 people in July 2021, although staffing fluctuated following security breaches ([Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization)).

Rapid7 independently describes the chats as showing recruitment interviews, coding exercises, salary negotiations, product discussions, and out-of-office messages. This evidence supports the characterization of Conti as an organization with human-resources and management practices resembling those of a legitimate software business, although its purpose was criminal ([Rapid7, 2022/2024](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/)).

The leaks also reportedly documented ongoing product improvement. CIS states that Conti allocated approximately $60,000 for a valid Cobalt Strike license, budgeted several thousand dollars per month for security and antivirus software used in testing, and redirected reverse-engineering work toward Windows 11. Rapid7 similarly reports that Conti tested endpoint-detection products and worked on technical problems such as encrypting very large files ([Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization); [Rapid7, 2022/2024](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/)).

### Scale, funding, and uncertainty

Rapid7 reports that the leaks exposed financial information, including a Bitcoin address that reportedly held more than $2 billion as of February 28, 2022. It also describes a conversation that appeared to indicate FSB involvement in part of Conti’s funding and interest in information concerning Bellingcat and Alexei Navalny. These points are reported as interpretations of leaked communications, not as adjudicated findings. The supplied source does not provide a court ruling independently confirming the alleged FSB relationship or the stated Bitcoin balance ([Rapid7, 2022/2024](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/)).

Accordingly, the strongest defensible conclusion is that the leaks demonstrated substantial organizational sophistication and apparent financial capacity. The more specific claims about state involvement and asset balances should remain qualified as reported or assessed rather than treated as proven facts.

## Public attribution and law-enforcement records

### RFJ’s alias and organizational attribution

RFJ offers a reward of up to $10 million for information leading to the identification or location of persons acting at the direction or control of a foreign government who participate in malicious cyber activity against U.S. critical infrastructure in violation of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. The page identifies Conti, also known as Wizard Spider, as a Russian government-linked RaaS group ([Rewards for Justice, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/)).

The same page lists five online aliases: “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis.” RFJ states that these actors are believed to be linked to Conti. It also associates Conti with TrickBot, IcedID, Cobalt Strike, and ZLoader. The wording—“believed to be linked”—signals an attribution assessment, not a judicial determination of identity or guilt ([Rewards for Justice, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/)).

### DOJ defendants and charges

The DOJ’s Middle District of Tennessee page identifies two cases. Case 3:23-CR-00092 names Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, and Andrey Zhuykov. Case 3:23-CR-00088 names Oleksii Lytvynenko. The DOJ states that the first group was charged with conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and conspiracy to commit wire fraud. It states that Lytvynenko was charged with conspiracy to deploy Conti ransomware, and the page records his June 10, 2026 guilty plea to Count 2, conspiracy to commit wire fraud ([U.S. Attorney’s Office, Middle District of Tennessee, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2)).

The DOJ page explicitly warns that defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. Therefore, the charges establish a formal law-enforcement allegation and a public case record, not an across-the-board adjudication of guilt. The supplied material confirms a guilty plea by Lytvynenko to the specified wire-fraud count, but it does not state that all named defendants were convicted.

### What cannot be established from the supplied record

The available evidence does not establish:

1. That any DOJ defendant was one of the RFJ aliases.
2. That the aliases correspond to specific legal names.
3. That every Conti-related actor participated in every operation.
4. That the reported FSB-related conversation proves direct state control of Conti.
5. That the number of victims in one source is directly comparable to the number in another.

These limits are not weaknesses in the overall attribution record; they are necessary distinctions between different types of public evidence.

## Assessment

The evidence supports a concrete conclusion: Conti was publicly described as a scalable, commercially organized ransomware enterprise whose core functions included malware development, testing, administration, recruitment, intrusion support, affiliate coordination, and extortion. The leaks materially strengthened that description by exposing internal labor specialization and management practices rather than merely showing the group’s public ransom demands.

The attribution record is also substantial but segmented. RFJ links the Conti/Wizard Spider organization to five online aliases through a government assessment. DOJ records separately connect five named defendants to Conti-related criminal allegations and, in Lytvynenko’s case, a reported guilty plea to conspiracy to commit wire fraud. The supplied sources do not bridge those two sets of identities. Any report that presents the aliases and defendants as identical would exceed the evidence.

## References

Center for Internet Security. (n.d.). *The Conti leaks: A case of cybercrime’s commercialization*. CIS. [https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization)

Rapid7. (2022, March 1; updated 2024, May 9). *Conti ransomware group internal chats leaked over Russia-Ukraine conflict*. Rapid7 Blog. [https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/)
